extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers of literary criticism, especially those interested in portraying or understanding heroic figures, prophets, and reformers in history and fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for representing Heroes, Prophets, Poets, and Reformers — what makes them effective, sincere, and historically consequential; also how audiences respond to them. Useful for writers crafting heroic characters or critics assessing heroic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet_vs_Reformer_mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the Poet's 'mild shining' from the Reformer’s 'fierce lightning' and employ each according to epochal need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'The mild shining of the Poet's light has to give place to the fierce lightning of the Reformer.' The finished Poet may be 'a symptom that his epoch itself has reached perfection and is finished'; when an age requires violent change, the Reformer rather than the Poet must act. Use Poetic, musical, or equable modes where culture is being harmonized; deploy Reforming, violent rhetoric when entrenched obstructions demand demolition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity_of_the_Reformer_when_obstructions_accumulate
rubrics_metrics.description: When previously indispensable institutions or representations become obstructions, a Reformer is necessary to shake them off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle explains that 'the very things that were once indispensable furtherances become obstructions; and need to be shaken off,' often with 'enormous difficulty.' In characterization or argument, make clear how old systems become dubitable and produce social pressure for revolutionary figures (e.g., Dante's representations dubitable to Luther).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality_as_enlargement_and_sincerity_over_novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is not mere novelty but the individual's enlargement of inherited views; sincerity, not newness, is the true merit of originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'Absolutely without originality there is no man... No man whatever believes, or can believe, exactly what his grandfather believed.' And: 'The merit of originality is not novelty; it is sincerity.' For writers: make characters' originality grounded in sincere conviction and development from received belief rather than contrived novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm_belief_required_for_effective_action
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who acts faithfully must 'believe firmly'; wavering belief produces unsound practice and ineffective, dishonest work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'At all turns, a man who will do faithfully, needs to believe firmly... If he have to ask at every turn the world's suffrage... he is a poor eye-servant; the work committed to him will be mis-done.' In depiction, show the link between internal conviction and the quality/effect of outward deeds; anti-pattern: characters who perform for appearance ('eye-servant') whose actions lead to cumulative offences and revolt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation_of_offences_leads_to_revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Dishonest, outward-looking practice accumulates offences until they 'become insupportable' and burst into violent revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle gives examples (Dante's Catholicism defaced by 'faithless, doubting and dishonest practice' leading to Luther). For narrative stakes: portray the gradual accrual of abuses and show tipping points where reformers or revolutions become inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity_of_essential_truth_through_formal_change
rubrics_metrics.description: Although forms and systems die, 'all death... is but of the body, not of the essence or soul'; an honest insight endures through changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'No thought that ever dwelt honestly as true in the heart of man but was an honest insight into God's truth... and has an essential truth in it which endures through all changes.' In writing/criticism avoid wholesale denigration of past beliefs; represent their essential contributions even as their forms are superseded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idolatry_and_its_true_evil_is_insincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Worship by symbols (idolatry) is ubiquitous; the fatal evil is insincere idolatry—'Cant' or 'Sincere-Cant'—when people 'only believe that they believe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'Condemnable Idolatry is insincere Idolatry... You do not believe, you only believe that you believe.' For characterization: distinguish sincere symbolic faith (which can be noble) from hypocritical formulaic worship that paralyzes moral life. Prophetic anger ought to be aimed at insincerity, not at all symbolic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero_as_idol-breaker_and_returner_to_reality
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hero (prophet/reformer) comes 'back to reality; that he stand upon things, and not shows of things,' acting to demolish hollow externals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'I find Luther to have been a Breaker of Idols... It is the property of every Hero... that he come back to reality.' In stories or essays, represent heroic gestures as acts restoring substance over semblance (e.g., Luther attacking Tetzel's indulgences). Anti-pattern: heroes who merely replace one form with another without restoring reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private_judgment_must_be_sincere_to_unite_not_anarchize
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise of private judgment, when sincere, does not produce isolation or anarchy but tends toward unity with others who hold truth sincerely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'The exercise of private judgment, faithfully gone about, does by no means necessarily end in selfish independence... it is error, insincerity, half-belief and untruth that make [anarchy].' For depiction: show characters who adopt received truths sincerely and thereby foster genuine community, versus insincere skeptics who fragment society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity_allows_borrowed_truths_to_be_genuine
rubrics_metrics.description: A person need not have personally discovered a truth to believe it sincerely; the 'believing man is the original man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'A man can believe, and make his own, in the most genuine way, what he has received from another.' When creating characters, allow them to be original in spirit through sincere adoption of inherited beliefs rather than forcing them to invent every conviction themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship_grounded_on_reality_and_sincerity_not_semblance
rubrics_metrics.description: True hero-worship and loyalty are founded on realities and sincerities, not on 'garnitures and semblances'; hence hero-worship 'never dies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle: 'Hero-worship never dies, nor can die... loyalty and Sovereignty are everlasting... grounded not on garnitures and semblances, but on realities and sincerities.' For writers: portray reverence for leaders as justified by their authentic moral strength, not by pomp or titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits_of_a_Heroic_Reformer (humble_origin_to_moral_courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exemplary reformer-hero often emerges from humble circumstances, suffers hardship, undergoes a conversion or conviction, reveres a revealed truth (e.g., the Bible), and displays moral courage to confront institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlyle sketches Luther: born poor, 'brought up poor... had to beg,' struck by friend's death, conversion via an old Latin Bible, then courageously confronting Tetzel and the Pope (burning the Bull, Diet of Worms). Use these elements as reliable markers of a compelling reformer-hero: humble roots, existential crisis, a founding revelation, and willingness to stand alone before power.
